focused_explanation.criterion: YES only if the response explicitly calls an idempotency key a unique identifier, token, or key sent with a request to identify the same logical operation across retries; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response explicitly says the server stores the key associated with the original result or response (for example, status and response body); otherwise NO.
YES only if the response explicitly says the key/result is retained for a limited time, gives a duration, or says it expires/is purged; otherwise NO.

YES only if the response explicitly says a retry with the same key returns/reuses the original result without executing the operation again AND contrasts that with an unprotected/new-key retry that repeats the operation or side effect; otherwise NO.

YES only if one concrete example states an initial operation succeeded but its response was lost/not received, a retry would duplicate the effect without a key, and reusing the same key prevents the second effect; otherwise NO.

short_how_to.criterion: YES only if the response gives a selection rule or concrete value for BOTH the connect timeout and the read timeout; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response says to retry transient failures (such as 5xx/network errors) and exclude non-transient/client failures (such as ordinary 4xx); otherwise NO.
YES only if the response names exponential backoff AND randomized jitter; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response explicitly names the Retry-After header and says to honor/respect its value; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response specifies a finite maximum retry/attempt count or a finite overall time limit; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response says a non-idempotent operation such as POST must not be retried unless the same idempotency key is used/provided; otherwise NO.
YES only if the response names a measurable retry-related signal (for example, retry rate or retries per request) that can expose misconfiguration; otherwise NO.
